what: Caesars Entertainment runs casinos. It owns and operates resorts on the Las Vegas Strip and dozens of regional casinos across the United States, and runs a digital business offering online sports betting and casino games. Its Caesars Rewards loyalty programme ties the whole estate together.
customers: Gamblers and leisure travellers at its resorts, conference and event organisers filling Las Vegas rooms midweek, and online sports bettors and casino players.
money: Casino, hotel, food and entertainment revenue from Strip properties.
Casinos across many states, serving mostly local and drive-in customers.
Online sports betting and iGaming, the growth business.
moat: Casino licences are granted by states and strictly limited, which keeps new competitors out of each regional market. Caesars Rewards is the real asset: a loyalty database spanning Las Vegas and dozens of regional properties lets the company bring a regional player to the Strip, which no single-property operator can do. Most of the real estate is leased rather than owned, which lowers the capital required but raises fixed costs.
risks: Debt is about $12.6B against a $6.0B market value and $887.0M of cash. The lenders’ claim is twice the size of the shareholders’.
The trailing twelve months show a net loss of about $533.0M, with interest costs consuming most of what the operations earn.
Much of the property is leased under long-term agreements with fixed, escalating rent, so the fixed cost base is high and does not fall when revenue does.
Regional casino revenue has been flat, and lower-income customers — the regional casino’s core — have been under pressure.
Fifteen analysts average a $31.27 target, only about 6% above the current price.
opportunities: Free cash flow of about $582.0M against a $6.0B market value is substantial, and the shares trade at about 10.3 times free cash flow and 5.2 times EV/EBITDA.
The digital business has moved from heavy losses to profitability, which removes the drag that defined the last few years.
Las Vegas demand has been resilient, supported by events, conferences and international visitors.
Any reduction in debt moves value directly to equity holders because the leverage is so high: a small improvement in enterprise value is a large one per share.
watch: Debt reduction and regional casino revenue. With borrowings at twice the market value of the equity, the path of the debt matters more to shareholders than anything happening on the casino floor.
view: The first thing to establish about Caesars is that this is not really a casino investment, it is a leveraged one. Debt of $12.6 billion sits against a $6.0 billion equity value, which means the lenders own twice as much of this enterprise as the shareholders do. Every pound of improvement in the business goes first to servicing that, and what reaches the equity is the residual. That is why the stock moves so violently on modest changes in expectations, and why the trailing net loss of $533 million exists despite the operations generating cash.

The operating business underneath is better than the loss suggests. Free cash flow of $582 million is real, EV/EBITDA of 5.2 is low, and the digital arm has finally crossed from being a cash incinerator to a contributor — which matters, because the losses there were a large part of why the last few years looked so poor. Las Vegas has held up on events, conferences and international visitors. The problem is the regional portfolio, where the customer is a local with a lower income, and that customer has been squeezed.

The structural feature people underweight is the leases. Caesars sold much of its real estate and now rents it back under long-term agreements with fixed, escalating rent. That lowered the capital needed to run the company and permanently raised the fixed cost base. In good years it magnifies returns; in a downturn the rent does not fall with revenue, which turns an operating problem into a solvency conversation faster than it would at an owner-operator. Anyone comparing Caesars with a casino company that owns its buildings is not comparing like with like.

So what is the bet? It is that the operations hold steady while the debt comes down, and that deleveraging transfers enterprise value to the equity — which with this much leverage is a powerful mechanism. It is a reasonable bet at 5.2 times EV/EBITDA. It is also a bet with no margin for a recession, because the fixed rent and the interest bill both carry on regardless. The fifteen analysts at barely 6% above the price are, I suspect, expressing exactly that discomfort. Watch the debt balance, not the gaming revenue.
bull: Regional revenue stabilises, the digital business keeps growing profitably, and steady debt reduction transfers enterprise value to a highly leveraged equity.
bear: The lower-income regional customer weakens further while fixed rent and a $12.6 billion interest bill carry on regardless, and the equity is the first thing squeezed.
